findings.claim: Removing the HTTP method restriction makes the middleware generate ETags and honor `If-None-Match` for unsafe methods (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), which can turn a mutating request's response into a `304 Not Modified`.
findings.rationale: Previously only GET/HEAD/QUERY reached the ETag logic. With the guard gone, a client that sends `If-None-Match` on a POST whose response body hashes to the same ETag gets a 304 with the body stripped, losing the mutation result. RFC 7232 also says `If-None-Match` on methods other than GET/HEAD should yield 412, not 304. Fairly confident this is a real regression unless a replacement guard exists further down the function (not visible in this hunk).

findings.claim: Removing `!c.res.ok` means error responses (4xx/5xx) and bodyless responses (204/205/304) now get ETags computed and can be converted to 304.
findings.rationale: An error body will now be hashed and an ETag attached; a client repeating the request with that `If-None-Match` receives a 304, which callers interpret as 'unchanged cached success' rather than a repeated error, silently swallowing error semantics. A response that is already 304/204 has no body, so hashing yields an ETag for empty content and may conflict with upstream cache headers. High confidence an explicit status check is still needed.

findings.claim: With both guards gone, every response — including streaming/SSE and very large bodies — now flows into ETag generation, which must buffer the body to hash it.
findings.rationale: ETag generation requires consuming the response body (typically via clone().arrayBuffer() downstream). Previously non-GET and non-ok responses short-circuited; now streamed responses (e.g. SSE from a POST endpoint) and large downloads would be fully buffered, breaking streaming and increasing memory use. Medium confidence — depends on how the code below handles bodyless/stream responses, which isn't shown in this hunk.
